summary: Background: Clinical notes are rich sources of clinical information and are routinely used in clinical practice to infer past diagnoses and other comorbidities. Large language models (LLMs) may simplify the task by extracting this information from clinical notes. Objective: The study aims to evaluate the performance of state-of-the-art LLMs on the task of labeling English clinical notes. Methods: This institutional review board–approved retrospective study comprised 380 clinical notes obtained from 2 institutions in the United States. The notes were manually labeled for the presence or absence of 29 conditions (simplified Elixhauser Comorbidity Index) by 2 human readers—a radiology resident and a medical student under the supervision of a senior radiologist. Forty-six LLMs, including 4 closed-source commercial models from the GPT and Claude families, and 42 open-weights LLMs from the Llama (13 models) and the Qwen (29 models) families were used to label each note. The GPT-o3-mini-high reasoning model was used to parse the free-text model responses to binary yes/no answers. Using the manual labels as the reference standard, the recall, precision, and -scores for the models were evaluated. The effect of factors such as the length of the notes and the family, size, and release recency of the LLMs was analyzed using generalized linear models. Results: The top-performing LLMs included the GPT and Claude models, and the larger open-weights models included Llama 3 70B, Llama 3.1 70B, Llama 3.1 405B, Llama 3.3 70B, Qwen 1.5 72B, Qwen 1.5 110B, Qwen 2 72B, and Qwen 2 VL 72B, which achieved -scores above 70%. The most recent and higher-capacity releases of the LLMs have been improving mainly in their precision. The evaluation of 29 conditions showed a large variance in performance depending on the condition. Conclusions: In this evaluation with 46 LLMs, larger open-weights LLMs such as the Llama 3.3 70B performed on par with or better than the GPT and Claude models, achieving -scores above 70%. The performance of open-weights models improved significantly with model size and recency. These results suggest that locally run open-weights LLMs can be potentially used to label clinical notes.
title: Labeling Clinical Notes With Large Language Models: Retrospective Benchmarking Study

summary: Richter and colleagues offer a careful systematic review of how large language model–based tools affect physician-patient communication, but the outcomes that matter most in deciding to scale a solution—trust and safety—are still unknown. Before deploying these tools, health systems need local validation, ongoing monitoring for accuracy and equity, and pragmatic trials that measure trust, safety, and outcomes alongside perceived empathy.
title: Is More Perceived Empathy Better? Large Language Models, Communication, and Safety in Health Care

summary: Background: The platform-based economy has expanded rapidly through the integration of digital platforms into sectors such as transportation, delivery, and freelance work. Platform labor combines features of precarious employment and digitalized work organization, encompassing both location-based and web-based work. Platform workers are often treated as a homogeneous group, despite substantial differences in job tasks, working conditions, and worker characteristics. Consequently, it remains unclear which health and safety risks are linked to shared features of platform-mediated work, and which reflect occupation-specific working conditions. Objective: This study aimed to compare how taxi drivers, delivery couriers, and online freelancers experience platform-specific and occupation-specific determinants of health, well-being, and safety, and to identify worker-informed solutions to address them. Methods: A participatory photovoice study was conducted with platform-based taxi drivers, delivery couriers, and freelancers living in Stockholm. Between September and November 2022, 16 participants were recruited through convenience sampling, operationalized through a targeted social media campaign, and divided into 3 occupation-specific groups (5‐6 participants per group). Each group participated in 5 weekly sessions involving photo documentation, group discussion, collaborative coding and analysis, and the development of themes and recommendations related to working conditions, health, and well-being. Results: Participants identified 14 themes representing major determinants of health, well-being, and safety at work, as well as 23 recommendations for improving working conditions. Workers reported exposure to both platform-specific risks, including algorithmic management and digital surveillance, and traditional occupational risks such as psychosocial strain, ergonomic challenges, and traffic-related hazards. Experiences differed substantially across platform work types. Delivery and taxi drivers reported greater exposure to physical and traffic-related risks, whereas freelancers emphasized psychosocial demands and digital work intensification. Economic insecurity and costs associated with maintaining work equipment emerged as common challenges across all groups. Attitudes toward flexibility, autonomy, and algorithmic management also varied between worker categories. Conclusions: This study highlights important similarities and differences in working conditions and health risks across platform work types. The findings suggest that research and occupational health interventions targeting platform workers should differentiate between specific forms of digital platform work to better capture the diversity of workers’ experiences and exposures.
title: Visualizing Health in Platform Work by Comparing Freelancers, Couriers, and Taxi Drivers in Sweden: Participatory Photovoice Study
From Reactive to Proactive Care: How AI Is Connecting Rio’s Residents to Public Services
Too Much Trust? Wearables and the Accuracy Perception Gap
When the Teaching Material Is the Risk: The Governance Gap for AI-Generated Content in Medical Education

summary: Intravenous fluid therapy is a cornerstone of optimizing body hydration, circulation, and perfusion, yet its rational implementation is limited by inconsistent clinical terminology. As fluid therapy moves toward AI-empowered clinical decision support systems (AI-CDSS), there is a critical need for high-quality, verified training data. The reliability of these systems is currently threatened by misleading data resulting from ambiguous definitions and the interchangeable use of nonsynonymous terms, such as “dehydration” and “hypovolemia.” This multidisciplinary panel-of-experts opinion article intends to start a discussion by identifying the key drawbacks in current terminology and proposes solutions, including a shift toward adequacy-based phenotypes and categorizing blood and water volumes as “insufficient,” “optimal,” or “excessive” rather than relying on context-sensitive quantitative measures such as “low,” “normal,” or “high.” Illustrative scenarios are used to show how inconsistent terminology and static quantitative labels could mislead an AI-CDSS. The proposed phenotype matrix is designed to provide a structured, systematic description of fluid requirements for specific clinical objectives that can be integrated into clinical algorithms and machine learning databases. An example of a fluid requirement assessment algorithm is used for exploring its applicability in AI training. The proposed terminology and phenotype matrix are provisional: they represent the opinion of a multidisciplinary expert panel and have not undergone formal consensus, clinical validation, or testing within an AI system. Broad consensus-building initiatives will follow.
title: Revising Terminology and Phenotype Definitions for AI-Based Decision Support in Fluid Therapy: Call for Consensus

summary: Clinical large language model agents depend on both model capability and the surrounding system that selects information, constrains actions, and verifies execution. In this Viewpoint, we argue that this harness should be an explicit unit of clinical agent design, evaluation, and reporting. Our aim is to help clinical informatics and development teams specify this layer and to help evaluators and institutional governance teams assess its contributions and risks. Selected benchmarks show substantial performance differences across harness configurations, but architecture comparisons, bundled improvements, and within-model component comparisons support different levels of causal attribution. We propose a revisable 3-tier framework: tier 1 specifies general orchestration functions, including prompts, tools, output schemas, control flow, memory, and generic verification; tier 2 specifies their clinical adaptations for knowledge integration, differential reasoning, missingness and temporality, safety verification, and workflow alignment; and tier 3 specifies a failure-driven evaluation cycle applied to both. Our contribution is a framework that makes these connections explicit. We provide classification rules, an illustrative clinical example, a proposed evaluation protocol, and a minimum reporting checklist. Observable execution traces are distinguished from private model reasoning, with provenance and privacy safeguards supporting retrospective reconstruction. Evaluation should separate task success, clinical correctness, process safety, and operational reliability. Lightweight fine-tuning can complement harness design; their interaction requires controlled study. The framework is a proposal for empirical testing, not a validated taxonomy or evidence of deployment safety.
title: Beyond Model Choice: A Harness-Centered Framework for Designing Clinical Large Language Model Agents

summary: AI-enabled digital medicine platforms in Europe are developed within overlapping rules for personal data, medical devices, AI, clinical research, health data access, and health technology assessment. This viewpoint represents the authors’ experience and interpretation from the preimplementation phase of INTERCEPT, an Innovative Health Initiative consortium that plans to validate biomarkers and develop a blood-based risk score for early Crohn disease interception. It does not report original empirical research, a systematic regulatory review, a deployed platform, or a validated AI model. Our aim is to explain how compliance-by-design can be translated into an auditable governance architecture and to identify what still requires scientific evaluation. We advance 3 messages. First, governance must begin with intended purpose and boundary mapping: a digital platform may contain research, operational, and medical device software functions, and conformity of one module cannot be inferred for the platform as a whole. Second, overlapping obligations can be operationalized through 5 linked controls: modular responsibility and change control, federated data governance, traceable AI life cycle management, consent and participant rights orchestration, and a common cross-border governance core with local adaptations. Third, compliance is not a surrogate for model validity, clinical benefit, trust, scalability, or market access. Before clinical deployment, planned AI components require prespecified labels and cohorts, leakage prevention, missing data and imbalance strategies, calibration, subgroup assessment, external validation, human factors evaluation, and postdeployment algorithmovigilance. A hypothetical biomarker risk score update illustrates how the 5 controls interact. INTERCEPT is informative because it combines cross-border biomarker research, planned predictive analytics, and heterogeneous institutional settings while key design decisions remain modifiable. Its contribution is nevertheless conceptual: the proposed framework is a testable governance hypothesis, not evidence of implementation success. Prospective studies should compare it with alternative governance models and assess safety, workload, participant experience, evidence generation, and regulatory performance.
title: Compliance-by-Design in an AI-Enabled Platform for Early Crohn Disease Interception: A Viewpoint

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> The proliferation of electronic clinical information resources has transformed how evidence is accessed during primary care consultations, particularly in community settings where clinicians must rapidly access reliable information at the point of care (POC). For general practice trainees, who are still developing clinical expertise and information-seeking skills, how these digital resources are used during real-time decision-making remains poorly understood. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aims to investigate the selection, use, and real-time interaction with electronic clinical information resources used by Australian general practice (GP) trainees (specialist vocational trainees in family medicine) during clinical decision-making. <strong>Methods:</strong> Using a novel qualitative interview and screen-capture approach, this study combines semistructured interviews with a screen-recorded, think-aloud protocol capturing real-time interaction with digital information systems. In 2024, a total of 20 GP trainees (women: n=13; men: n=7) in their final 2 years of GP specialty training participated in the study, first discussing their general approaches to information seeking, followed by a live, video-recorded task session where participants engaged with hypothetical clinical vignettes using their usual information resources. Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. GP trainees from various community-based training practices across Australia were purposively sampled to capture diverse perspectives within primary care settings. <strong>Results:</strong> GP trainees relied on a combination of personal knowledge, clinical guidelines, and electronic information resources during decision-making. Major themes included a desire to “do the right thing” while under constraints of other themes such as time limits and perceived patient perception. Think-aloud sessions revealed common patterns in information resource selection, and that trainees often struggled with the efficiency and accessibility of finding specific information. Trainees sometimes made errors in information synthesis and judgment. Trainees frequently used a stepped approach to choosing internet resources and preferred resources that provided quick, reliable answers, indicating a preference for accessible information resources over comprehensive but time-consuming evidence repositories. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Trainees used rapid, pragmatic strategies centered on trusted resources to support decision-making within significant time and contextual constraints. While trainees endorsed the principles of evidence-based medicine, the realities of POC practice limited direct engagement with the underlying evidence base. These findings suggest that current electronic clinical resources may require redesign to better integrate with clinical workflows and present clinically relevant evidence in ways that support timely, evidence-informed decision-making in primary care.
title: The Use of Electronic Information Resources by General Practice Trainees During Consultations in Australia: Qualitative Analysis of Interview and Screen-Recording Data
